intro: Michael Laucke fits the first Gymnopédie onto six guitar strings. The bass, the softly plucked chords and the long melody all belong to one pair of hands.

cues.title: Satie on six strings
cues.text: Laucke’s guitar carries the low bass, the accompanying chords and the melody. Satie spaces them apart: bass on beat one, chord on beat two, then long melody notes above. Each pluck begins to fade while the next note is being made.
cues.evidence: Satie, Gymnopédie No. 1, Dover edition, bars 1–12, transcribed for Mutopia. Laucke’s arrangement and performance are credited on the recording page. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37 ; https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Satie_Gymnopedie_No_1_performed_by_Michael_Laucke.flac
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: A lower melody note
cues.text: The melody drops lower and holds a single note while the chords beneath it change. The accompaniment keeps its slow three-beat step. Satie can darken a phrase without making it hurry.
cues.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, bars 17–21. The section boundary follows this passage in Laucke’s transposed arrangement; the piano score supplies the melodic and harmonic design. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bass starts again
cues.text: The first ending has settled in major. Now the opening bass-and-chord pattern returns, with space above it before the melody comes back. The same tune makes a second circuit.
cues.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, first ending and return to bars 1–5. The recording’s established section boundary places the return here. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The darker ending
cues.text: The closing melody changes one of its long notes: the major third falls a semitone. Satie’s second ending closes in minor, leaving the same bass destination with a different chord above it.
cues.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, second ending, bars 40–47; compare bars 32–39. Laucke transposes the work from the piano original. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A held note crosses changing chords
transitions.from: A · Bass and softly plucked chords
transitions.how: The melody drops to a lower held note, and the bass leaves its opening alternation. In the piano score, E minor becomes E minor seventh, then D minor under the held E. Laucke carries this change into the guitar arrangement, keeping the slow bass-on-one, chord-on-two rhythm.
transitions.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, piano bars 17–21; chord names refer to the original key. The section boundary locates the corresponding passage in Laucke’s transposed arrangement. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37

transitions.title: The accompaniment starts again
transitions.how: The first ending closes in major. The accompaniment then starts afresh, with a low bass note followed by a seventh chord. Four bars of this pattern prepare the melody. Satie leaves the upper line empty while the bass finds its familiar step.
transitions.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, bars 38–39 followed by the return to bars 1–5. The guitar arrangement is transposed. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37

transitions.title: The third falls a semitone
transitions.to: B′ · The ending turns to minor
transitions.how: The repeated melody takes Satie’s second ending. Its long major third is flattened, and the accompanying chords change with it. In the piano original, F♮ replaces F♯ over a repeated E bass; the last chord closes in D minor. The guitar carries the same major-to-minor turn in its transposed key.
transitions.evidence: Dover edition, Mutopia transcription, alternatives at bars 32–39 and 40–47; the note names describe the piano original. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=37

composer.epithet: The composer of the Gymnopédies asked pianists to prepare for 840 repetitions with ‘serious immobilities’.
facts: Paris Conservatoire; returned to study at the Schola Cantorum in 1905, aged thirty-nine
Honfleur, then Montmartre; a room in Arcueil from 1898 until his death
Cocteau, Picasso and Massine for Parade; Picabia and René Clair for Relâche
Piano miniatures, songs, ballets, Socrate and the comic Memoirs of an Amnesiac
composer.background:
In April 1912 Erik Satie informed the readers of the Revue musicale S.I.M. that he preferred measuring sounds to hearing them. His equipment had yielded alarming results. A B♭ examined through a phonoscope was so repulsive that he summoned his servant to look; an ordinary F♯, emitted by a large tenor, weighed ninety-three kilograms. “I get more pleasure from measuring a sound than from hearing it,” he explained. The essay belonged to his Memoirs of an Amnesiac. Musical science had acquired a wonderfully unreliable witness.

He was born in Honfleur in 1866, the son of a French shipping broker and an English mother of Scottish descent. After she died in 1872, he and his brother returned from Paris to their paternal grandparents in Normandy. A local organist, Gustave Vinot, taught him music and introduced him to plainchant. Back in Paris, Satie entered the Conservatoire in 1879. Two periods of study produced dismal reports and no diploma.
